stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

on the last line of your reply:

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown

many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.

- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.

---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for Continual-ARC puzzles. Infer grid rules from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC Puzzle Solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid tasks presented as a stream, especially when the interface charges for both wrong submissions and demo requests.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the grid and inventory objects.** Record dimensions, background color, and each non-background connected component: color, bounding box, area, and rough shape. Treat each test instance as independent; do not assume prior session examples are available.
2. **Diff every demonstration exactly.** Compare input and output cell by cell. Identify precisely which cells changed and which stayed fixed. Group changed cells into components and note whether the change is recoloring, movement, copying, deletion, or shape construction.
3. **Infer the rule from object relationships, not isolated colors.** Look for repeated shape motifs, matching silhouettes, marker/reference objects, alignment, symmetry, size, and adjacency. Use all demos to distinguish competing hypotheses; a single changed component may be consistent with several rules.
4. **Apply the hypothesis to the test.** Predict the complete output grid, preserving every cell not implicated by the rule. Check row/column indexing and dimensions before submitting.
5. **Choose demos strategically.** Request another pair when plausible rules would produce different test outputs and the expected value of disambiguation exceeds the cost. Prefer a demo that reveals whether selection depends on shape, color, position, or a reference marker. Avoid requests that merely repeat evidence already available.
6. **Submit only after validating.** Confirm output dimensions, legal values 0–9, and that edits are limited to the predicted target(s). Since a wrong submission costs a point, use the available evidence rather than guessing when the hypothesis is weak.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume every occurrence of a color is transformed: demonstrations can show untouched components of the same color.
- Do not interpret a changed component by color alone. A reference shape or relation among shapes may determine which object changes.
- Preserve the exact geometry of a selected object unless the demos show a geometric operation; recoloring typically changes only its cells.
- Do not accidentally alter background cells, neighboring objects, or visually similar but non-selected components.
- Avoid submitting an unchanged grid merely because the rule is unclear; use an informative demo when the remaining uncertainty affects the answer.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Each demo's changed coordinates have been identified exactly.
- [ ] The rule explains both changed and unchanged objects.
- [ ] The chosen test object(s) satisfy the rule.
- [ ] Predicted output has the original dimensions and only justified edits.
